## Working out the components from the known tasks

**Y components** (found by checking which bit position separates the button outcomes):
- **Y1 is bit 3.** In X5-Y1-Z2, button 2 appears exactly when bit 3 is 1 in both stimuli.
- **Y4 is bit 1.** In X5-Y4-Z2, button 2 appears exactly when bit 1 is 1 in both stimuli.
- **Y2 is bit 2.**
  - In X4-Y2-Z4, button 1 appears exactly when bit 2 is the same in both stimuli.
  - In X3-Y2-Z1, button 3 appears exactly when bit 2 is 0 in both stimuli.

**X5:** The rule splits "both are 1" from everything else. So X5 is either "both are 1" or "not both are 1", and Z2 orients the buttons to match. Both options fit both X5 tasks.

**X3, X4 and Z1** are linked through the shared Z components. Two chains fit every example:
- **Chain A:**
  - X4 is "same", so Z4 gives 1 when true.
  - That makes X3 "at least one", so Z1 gives 0 when true and 3 when false.
  - Check: X4-Y2-Z1 gives 0 when bit 2 matches, as required.
- **Chain B:**
  - X4 is "exactly one", so Z4 gives 2 when true.
  - That makes X3 "neither", so Z1 gives 3 when true and 0 when false.
  - Check: this is also consistent with X4-Y2-Z1.

The choice of X5 is independent of the choice of chain, so there are 4 joint assignments. They produce only two distinct predictions for X5-Y1-Z1:
- **Prediction (i):** bit 3 is 1 in both stimuli gives 0; otherwise 3.
- **Prediction (ii):** bit 3 is 1 in both stimuli gives 3; otherwise 0.

The examples cannot tell these apart, so the answer is not determined. I'm going with (i), which uses X5 = "both are 1" and Chain A.

## Predictions

Bit 3 is 1 in both stimuli only for inputs 5, 8 and 13, so those get 0 and all others get 3.

| # | Input | Bit 3 pair | Button |
|---|-------|-----------|--------|
| 1 | 0101 0000 | 0,0 | 3 |
| 2 | 0000 1001 | 0,0 | 3 |
| 3 | 1101 1001 | 0,0 | 3 |
| 4 | 1000 1100 | 0,0 | 3 |
| 5 | 1011 1010 | 1,1 | 0 |
| 6 | 0100 1110 | 0,1 | 3 |
| 7 | 0000 0110 | 0,1 | 3 |
| 8 | 0111 0011 | 1,1 | 0 |
| 9 | 0101 0100 | 0,0 | 3 |
| 10 | 0110 1100 | 1,0 | 3 |
| 11 | 0001 1111 | 0,1 | 3 |
| 12 | 0110 0101 | 1,0 | 3 |
| 13 | 0110 1010 | 1,1 | 0 |
| 14 | 1001 0111 | 0,1 | 3 |
| 15 | 1101 1011 | 0,1 | 3 |
| 16 | 1101 0011 | 0,1 | 3 |

Prediction (ii) would swap every 0 and 3. With two equally supported outcomes, my confidence that all 16 answers are right is about 50%.

# Learn tasks from examples

Each task maps an input to one of four buttons: 0, 1, 2, or 3. An input is a pair of stimuli; each stimulus has 4 binary features, written as 4 bits (bit positions 1-4, left to right). The line `1011 0110 -> 2` means: stimulus 1 is 1011, stimulus 2 is 0110, and the correct button is 2.

Every task is built from three components. A **Y component** picks one of the 4 features (bit positions 1-4); the task looks at that feature in both stimuli. An **X component** is a rule on those two bits, one of: both are 1; at least one is 1; exactly one is 1; neither is 1; not both are 1; both are the same. A **Z component** gives one button when the rule is true and a different button when it is false. A task's label lists its components, for example X2-Y1-Z3. Each kind has several versions (X1, X2, and so on); different versions of a kind are different from each other, and the same label always means the same component. You are not told which version does what.
